input:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy provides an elegant and widely used link between momentum transfer and mass transfer, setting the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to one half of the friction factor, in the form $j_D$ = $f/2$, for the same geometry and the same flow conditions. In other words, the analogy effectively allows a friction measurement to stand in for a mass-transfer coefficient, so that one transport quantity can be read directly from the other, which is a considerable practical convenience. A brief numerical check illustrates the arithmetic involved: at $f$ = 0.046, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.046 / 2 = 0.023. It should be noted that no measurement enters into this step, and the value of 0.023 is simply the friction result restated in mass-transfer form.

However, it is important to recognise that the analogy holds only where the resistance to momentum transfer and the resistance to mass transfer are located in the same place. It breaks down where part of the friction arises from form drag, since a rough surface, or a body that sheds a wake, expends momentum on pressure forces that have no direct counterpart in mass transfer. In such cases, the measured $f$ overstates the portion of the resistance that the analogy is able to use, and $j_D$ consequently falls below $f/2$, with the shortfall growing as the share of form drag in $f$ increases.
target:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor, $j_D$ = $f/2$, for the same geometry and flow. Stated in that form, the analogy lets a friction measurement stand in for a mass-transfer coefficient: one transport quantity is read from the other. A short check shows the arithmetic the analogy asks for. At $f$ = 0.046, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.046 / 2 = 0.023. No measurement enters that step; the value 0.023 is the friction result restated in mass-transfer form.

The analogy holds where the resistance to momentum transfer and the resistance to mass transfer sit in the same place. It fails where part of the friction comes from form drag. A rough surface, or a body that sheds a wake, spends momentum on pressure forces that have no counterpart in mass transfer, and the measured $f$ then overstates the part of the resistance the analogy can use. In that case $j_D$ falls below $f/2$, and the shortfall grows with the share of form drag in $f$. For such surfaces the measured $f$ cannot be halved into a mass-transfer factor, because part of $f$ was never a transfer resistance at all.
